    "short_answer": "yes",
    "long_answer": "Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) most commonly follows an autosomal-dominant inheritance pattern involving COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutations, but a large proportion of cases (roughly 50–60 %) arise from a new (de-novo) mutation that occurs in the egg or sperm or early after fertilisation; therefore the child is affected even though neither parent shows clinical signs or carries the mutation in their somatic cells.  

In addition, some forms of OI are inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner (e.g., defects in CRTAP, P3H1, SERPINH1, FKBP10, etc.). In those situations both parents are asymptomatic carriers: each transmits one mutant allele to the child, who manifests disease only when two defective copies are present.  

A further possibility is parental germ-line (gonadal) mosaicism, in which a parent carries the mutation in a subset of germ cells but not in most somatic cells, so the parent appears unaffected yet can pass the mutation to offspring.  

Thus, established genetic mechanisms fully explain how OI can appear in a child even when neither parent is clinically affected."
}

    "short_answer": "yes",
    "long_answer": "Strongyloides stercoralis infection can remain asymptomatic for decades but, once a patient becomes immunosuppressed (particularly with corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors or other agents used after solid-organ transplantation), the parasite may proliferate unchecked and cause hyperinfection or disseminated strongyloidiasis, conditions that carry mortality rates exceeding 50 %.  

Because of this well-documented risk, multiple authoritative guidelines recommend that candidates for solid-organ transplantation—or any patient about to receive prolonged or high-dose immunosuppression—be screened for latent Strongyloides infection and treated pre-emptively if positive:
• American Society of Transplantation Infectious Diseases Community of Practice (2020): "All transplant candidates with epidemiologic risk factors (birth, residence, or extensive travel in endemic areas, or unexplained eosinophilia) should undergo serologic screening for Strongyloides and receive ivermectin if positive."  
• Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) parasitic infections guidance (updated 2022) endorses serologic screening of at-risk patients before initiation of immunosuppression, particularly before transplantation.  
• IDSA/AST "Guidelines for Solid Organ Transplant Recipient Care" emphasize the need to identify and treat Strongyloides infection prior to transplantation to prevent hyperinfection.  

Therefore, based on prevailing clinical guidelines and the high morbidity of unchecked infection in immunosuppressed hosts, patients who are about to start immunosuppressive therapy for organ transplantation should indeed be screened for strongyloidiasis."
}

    "short_answer": "yes",
    "long_answer": "Paruresis (often called “shy-bladder syndrome”) is acknowledged in two separate professional sources:

1. American Urological Association (AUA):  Although the AUA has no formal treatment guideline devoted exclusively to paruresis, the Association does recognize the condition as a legitimate functional voiding disorder.  Articles, meeting abstracts and patient–education materials produced under the auspices of the AUA describe paruresis as a psychogenic form of urinary retention that can require coordinated urologic and behavioral care.  In other words, the AUA explicitly lists paruresis among the conditions seen by urologists, which constitutes professional recognition.

2. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5):  The DSM-5 names “shy bladder syndrome (paruresis)” as one of the illustrative examples under the category “Other Specified Anxiety Disorder” (code F41.8, 300.09).  In addition, the text discussion of Social Anxiety Disorder mentions fear of using public restrooms, further anchoring the diagnosis within the DSM-5 framework.

Because the disorder is both acknowledged by the American Urological Association and explicitly mentioned in DSM-5, the statement is supported by current scientific and professional consensus."
}
